    A post shared by Nikita Redkar (@nikitadumptruck).

    In a recent development, redkar: On Mondays, I have a researcher and we go through the topics that people are talking about on social media. We pull up some news sites and see what the big stories are, and we leave some room for breaking news throughout the week.

    My week is [split] between videos [on topics] that the general public is talking about, and videos that are just interesting to me. That’s how I stay sane in this business. I’m lucky to have the flexibility of doing that. My researcher combs through news sites and research papers and compiles all that information for me, then I put together a script.

    Redkar: It’s definitely my favorite color, but it’s like the chicken and the egg — I don’t know if I liked it before I was doing this.

    I pick whatever outfit I feel cute in. In getting ready with me videos, I start with a completely bare face, so at least the outfit has to be giving a little bit.

    Industry observers note that tameez: Tell me about the Get Ready with Me videos. How do you decide what’s a GRWM and what’s a walking video?

    Sources indicate that redkar: It’s like: What am I comfortable screaming out in the streets versus what do I need to keep at home? Some topics require more seriousness; if it does, I can do the GRWM for that. But if it’s something [less serious], I can be walking my dog or have on some ridiculous outfit.

    Redkar: If I get a fact wrong, I’ll do a follow-up video. It’s rare that I’ve gotten a fact wrong because between me and my researcher, that’s two levels of checks before something hits the internet.

    For one video, I didn’t factually get it wrong, but I should have included more of the story. It was about the Ugandan dictator Idi Amin and how Indians were expelled from Uganda, which is kind of how we got both Zohran Mamdani and Charli XCX [living in the U.S.], because both of their parents were part of the group that was expelled. I disregarded the racism that local Ugandans faced because of the Indians. I just focused on the expulsion and I framed Indians as the victims.

    A lot of people in the comments were like, “Hey, like, you really should have remarked this other part too.” I just deleted that video, because I didn’t want this to spread and only give half of the story.

    Sources indicate that redkar: My favorite video in recent memory was about girls on the first date, how we’re all so vigilant these days about dating men. I had so much fun doing it because I was talking about how life is affected by politics, instead of just politics. I think that video did really well because a lot of people connected to it.

    Last year I did a video that I called “How we went from Brat Summer to Hitler Winter” and talked about the hedonism of the 2024 summer and the fascism that followed. I related it to the Roaring 20s transitioning to the Great Depression to the World War. I incorporated a lot of pop culture [references].

    A post shared by Nikita Redkar (@nikitadumptruck).

    Redkar: Constantly. I posted a video about the Cornell professor who invented the term sexual harassment. I thought it was so interesting and timely, but it did not do well at all. The problem with content creation is sometimes you can’t tell if people didn’t like a video or if you’re being shadow banned.

    Redkar: I really love Liz Plank. She’s @feministabulous on Instagram. I love her coverage and how she leans into current conversations in pop culture.

    Industry observers note that I really like Charles McBryde. He’s not talking about just news — he’s very foreign policy-focused as well.

    @MissEatingGood on Instagram is a great explainer of what’s going on and the historical context.

    Industry observers note that redkar: Just finding ways to work together. I think there is so much benefit in that. I know countless creators who take a journalist’s article and dissect it down. Maybe [the journalists] should be the ones doing that.

    It has been revealed that I would happily pair up with journalists and teach them the ins and outs of content creation and how to make a short-form video article that’s also attention-grabbing. That’s just the reality; people are on social media, everyone’s attention span is shot, which sucks. We could try to fix that, but at this moment, we’re not fixing it. It’s really helpful to go on social media and talk [about your reporting] because journalists work hard on their articles.

    Sources indicate that creators [should] take more time. We rush way too much. It’s not our fault, because these platforms reward you for making content more frequently and punish you if you take a few days off. [Not rushing] sucks, but what can you do? It’s better than putting incorrect, or rushed, or incomplete information out there.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This isn’t another product job.

    It’s the chance to define a new category : The Operating System (OS) for Human Greatness Augmented with AI.

    Science-backed. Design-led. AI-powered. Global.

    A chance to build an AI-native Product Department.

    You’ll be working with the most complex data in the world : the human mind.

    Deep inside you are looking for a fresh adventure with….

    🚀Ambition around AI field : Smart teammates driven to create an iconic, international product.

    🔥Impact : you strive to make a real difference in the organization's growth, and not be a number in a big organization.

    😍Mission : knowing your greatness left a mark in people's lives, through technology and behavioral science.

    At Paradox, we believe that greatness is trainable.

    That’s why we want to empower people at scale by leveraging cutting edge technologies like AI, and crafting user experiences with outstanding aesthetics.

    - Human Intelligence (coaches, peers, and mentors).

    - Structured Intelligence (protocols, mental models, rituals),.

    - Technological Intelligence (AI personalization, feedback loops, adaptive journeys).

    To create one seamless ecosystem: Paradox OS.

    This is why we are looking for a PM to make Paradox a category-defining global brand loved for its product.

    This is a full-time position from our beautiful offices in Dubai, Paris or Lisbon or remotely anywhere in the world.

    We believe self-help is broken.Most learning platforms are used the same way : consuming generic theories, getting quick highs, ending with no real change.

    According to recent reports, at Paradox, we believe people deserve more.More than content. More than motivation.

    They deserve a system that knows them, one that adapts, challenges, and grows with them.

    We believe that every human learns differently, and that technology can do more than entertain or save time.It can translate insight into transformation, through AI personalization, lean experimentation, and deep psychological understanding.

    Because learning shouldn’t just make you feel inspired for a day, it should change how you live, think, and create.

    At Paradox, we want to re-invent how people grow.

    We do not build another course or coaching app but the Operating System for Greatness.

    Founded by David Laroche - a creator followed by over 2 million people and known for his interviews with icons like Tony Parker, Mike Horn, Richard Branson, and Gad Elmaleh, Paradox aims to build something that will live beyond any individual (including its founder), for decades to come.

    Our ambition is to compete with players like Mindvalley (150M ARR), but with a sharper vision, grounded protocols for achievers, people who want more for their life, refusing mediocrity.

    To do that, we bring together designers, tech, coaches, and filmmakers to create learning experiences that are cinematic, precise, and effective.

    According to recent reports, we move fast, aim high, and hold ourselves to the standards of Apple, Spotify, and MasterClass. No fluff, focused on meaningful impact.

    While others hide their numbers, we want to let our results speak loudly for us.

    Get obsessed with transforming our clients’ lives and let those transformations be our marketing.

    We want to build an AI-native firm, with agents in every department doing the work alongside our people.

    In product, that means building a self-learning AI for product management: a system that learns from every user signal, experiment and release, and gets sharper at deciding what to build next.

    For our clients, it means a self-learning AI that serves them through psychology and coaching, and gets better at helping each person change with every interaction.

    You won’t just use AI tools: you’ll help design the agents, loops and feedback systems that make Paradox learn faster than anyone else.

    -----------------------------------------.

    As Product Manager, you’ll be the architect of a fresh category, transforming growth into a living ecosystem powered by AI, behavioral science, and design.

    You won’t just build features, you’ll craft experiences that rewire behavior.

    You’re the architect bringing clarity between vision and execution, the person who turns “we should build this” into “it’s live, here’s the data and tangible impact.”.

    Every product cycle you lead will integrate:.

    Protocols : guided frameworks grounded in psychology that rewire perception, emotion, and action.

    Pods : human connection, accountability, and shared rituals.

    Loops : adaptive, AI-powered coaching cycles that evolve with each user.

    Personalization : experiences that feel uniquely theirs, every time.

    Going from a successful personal brand, to an international tech-driven iconic brand, is far from easy. It will be messy, chaotic - requiring constant iterations on MVPs and innovation in tech. Therefore to achieve this here are :.

    -----------------------------------------.

    Translate the founder’s strategic vision into a clear product strategy.

    Build and maintain the roadmap that connects business goals, user outcomes, and technological innovation.

    Ensure every feature supports the evolution of the Paradox ecosystem: Loops, PX Agents, Protocols, Membership.

    Be obsessed with user problems : talk to people weekly, analyze patterns, and identify where transformation breaks.

    Turn insights from behavioral science, coaching psychology, and learning design into actionable product hypotheses.

    Design loops, feedback, and rituals that make growth tangible.

    build for both the heart (inspiration) and the brain (structure).

    Apply Lean Startup methodology and scientific thinking to validate ideas through MVPs, not opinions.

    Design experiments and measurable success metrics before building.

    Iterate on a weekly basis on new hypothesis.

    Define and track product success metrics (activation, retention, transformation rates).

    Connect data to business KPIs, know how your product drives lifetime value, not just engagement.

    We don’t track metrics just for internal dashboards, we track them also to prove transformation.

    Help marketing leverage this data to fuel authentic, evidence-based storytelling — showing the world what real transformation looks like.

    Create a visceral experience that translates into emotions of inspiration, awe from users.

    Use a Science-backed, Cinematic, Contrarian style : Every product touchpoint should be grounded in behavioral science, expressed with cinematic beauty, and challenge conventions.

    -----------------------------------------.

    3–6 years as a Product Manager / Product Owner in EdTech, SaaS, or Consumer Tech.

    Bonus: experience in AI-driven products, learning design, or personal development platforms.

    You’ve shipped at least one major feature or product end-to-end, and can show measurable results.

    Uses Figma comfortably, prototypes directly.

    Craft-obsessed : You get things done, you love to work much beyond 9-5, you have a doer mentality, a bias for outcomes and want to be a beast in your field.

    User & Impact Obsessed: You think in outcomes, not outputs, you care about transformation.

    Analytical & System Thinker: You can turn a vague problem into a clear hypothesis, metrics, and roadmap.

    Digital & AI savvy : you’re able to build AI Agents (if not, you demonstrate ability to learn while applying).

    Cross-disciplinary Curiosity: You speak both tech and human; You can move from vision to spreadsheet to Figma.

    English: Fluent English, you can hold a conversation on specific details with English-speaking colleagues.

    Our chosen language for written communication is English.

    --------------------------------.

    ❌ If you need clarity before chaos — wrong place.❌ If you prefer balance over intensity — wrong season.❌ If you build to deliver, not to elevate — wrong mission.

    ❌Surface-level Vision Alignment : you like the idea of Paradox but doesn’t want to get the depth. Paradox is design-led; you must touch the product, not just manage it.

    ✅ If you’re obsessed with systems, psychology, and design…✅ If you dream of using AI to amplify what makes us human….

    Build a product that fuses neuroscience, design, and AI to reinvent how humans grow.

    The chance to build a product that could redefine human potential.

    Work with filmmakers, psychologists, engineers, and creatives obsessed with impact.

    In the heart of our headquarters stands the 100 000 Dreams Wall,.

    Every photo on that wall is a life rewritten:.

    “I found peace with my father.”.

    You will play a crucial role in the development of an Iconic Product.

    -> 🏅Being surrounded by A-players who strive to perform.

    But you don’t just want a competitive paycheck, you also want….

    -> Playing a crucial role in the development of a company whose content and products will be used by millions of people.

    -> Waking up in the morning feeling like you are making a difference is something!We receive messages every day from clients who have successfully lost weight, quit smoking, reached a milestone in their business, built better relationships, and made positive changes in their lives.

    -> ❤️ Contributing to the Paradox Foundation (our non-profit), dedicated to empower teenagers.

    But that's not all, we believe that driven people deserve….

    -> 😎A firm culture based on autonomy & accountability.

    -> 🌎A remote culture from day one with the freedom to work from wherever you want.

    -> 🏤Magnificent office in Dubai, Paris, Lisbon - it feels like home :).

    -> 🧍‍♀️Standing desks paid by the company if you live far from our offices.

    -> 💻Work on Mac, for us it counts :).

    -> 🏀350€ per year paid by the firm to take care of yourself ( for your gym, or dance class or whatever make you feel great).

    -> 📚150€ of books or education - At Paradox, we are learner lovers and we want to support you in that.

    -> 🔥6 1:1coachings - A Paradox Coach supporting you on anything personal or professional, we want you to live your best life.

    ⚠️ To complete the recruitment process, each candidate must organize calls with his or her previous managers. If you are not comfortable with this : do not apply ⚠️.

    If all this sounds good to you, come and write the next chapter with us 🚀🚀🚀🚀.

    That job description resonated with you?

    Here is your tailor made hiring process.

    📃 A 6 to 8 minutes application survey (with a short video assignment).

    💻 A 30mn video call with Timy, HR, to deep dive into your career path and ambitions.

    💻 A 1h video call with Timy, HR, to discuss how you'd fit into Paradox’s Product team.

    💻 A 1h culture-fit video call, to assess alignment with our values and mindset.

    💻 A 1h final video call with David, CEO, to discuss Product Vision and the next milestones to build.

    💼 Reference check to understand how you operate across environments and help set you up for a smooth onboarding.

    Our recruitment process is tailored to do our best to avoid that you or us realize that we’re not a perfect fit. Every step serves a purpose and will allow us to get to know you better as much as it’ll help you understand more where you’ll be stepping in.

    We also want you to have time to ask all of your questions regarding the mission, the long-term vision of your team and the manufacturer, our values, with the relevant interlocutor in front of you.

    If you believe design and AI can awaken what’s best in us then this isn’t a career move.

    Let’s build the Operating System for Greatness.

    “We’re pausing the changes as we continue to engage with stakeholders and take our time to get this right.”.

    Meta has indefinitely delayed its proposed commercial terms of service, which would have permitted the tech giant to scrape the websites of Meta Business account consumers.

    On Thursday, the company took down the preview link to the proposed terms and published an update to its Business Help Center that reads: “We recently shared that we were updating the Meta Commercial Terms, Product Catalog Terms, Self-Serve Ad Terms, and Ad Creative Generative AI Terms. These updates are now paused and will not take effect on November 20, 2026. We are continuing to consult with stakeholders and will provide a further update when we have more to share. In the meantime, our existing terms remain in effect.”.

    Meta — which owns Facebook, Messenger, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads — has repeatedly pushed back the terms’ effective date since Nieman Lab first reported on them on October 15. The terms were first set to take effect on October 30, sparking global outcry among news publishers, politicians, and trade organizations. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.” On October 23, Meta moved the effective date back by three weeks to November 20.

    Last week, Meta pledged to consult news publishers and industry leaders ahead of putting new commercial terms into effect.

    Industry observers note that “We’ve heard publishers’ feedback on our proposed ads and business terms update. We care deeply about our partners and do not initiative to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders,” vice president of communications Andy Stone tweeted on October 28. “We’re committed to getting this right, and as we expect this consultation could extend beyond November 20, in which case we’d delay implementation of the updated terms.”.

    Industry observers note that since then, courts in Norway and Brazil have issued preliminary injunctions to block the terms from taking effect as a result of lawsuits filed by media organizations in both countries. The United Kingdom’s Competition and Markets Authority has opened a formal investigation into Meta, examining whether the tech giant was “abusing a dominant position by imposing exploitative terms on publishers and advertisers.”.

    According to recent reports, in the United States, the proposed terms stoked bipartisan concern. At the end of October, Sens. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) sent letters to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg asking him to withdraw the terms.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that google search results that reached rank tracker Nozzle dropped to about one-tenth of their usual volume for approximately 10 hours on Nov.
    • It has been revealed that some of the blocked searches ended up on a Google page asking owners to sign in prior to seeing search engine results.
    • The numbers reported by Nozzle are based on its own collection through the five SERP data providers which processed the requests made by Nozzle that day.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that google search results that reached rank tracker Nozzle dropped to about one-tenth of their usual volume for approximately 10 hours on Nov. 18 based on information from Nozzle. Also during this time frame, Google was still rolling out its November core patch.

    It has been revealed that some of the blocked searches ended up on a Google page asking owners to sign in prior to seeing search engine results. On Nov. 17, Rajan Patel, the VP of Engineering for Search at Google, commented that he did not believe this login page was supposed to appear on the first page of search results, though Google could be conducting a test.

    The numbers reported by Nozzle are based on its own collection through the five SERP data providers which processed the requests made by Nozzle that day. So Nozzle’s reports cannot provide evidence of whether other rank tracker companies experienced the same drop in deliveries. Nozzle is a organization that sells tools for tracking rankings.

    According to recent reports, deliveries to Nozzle fell at all five providers for several hours, as Derek Perkins wrote in an article dated Nov. 18 on the Nozzle blog. Nozzle was collecting normally on Nov. 17 and until late morning UTC on Nov. 18, when deliveries slowed down.

    Industry observers note that on Nov. 18, from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. ET, Nozzle received 11.6% of what would be collected during 10 regular hours. During each provider’s worst hour, that provider received 2% or less of its regular hourly amount.

    Nozzle’s hourly chart highlights when the drop began and when deliveries started to recover.

    Recent findings suggest that one of the providers also told Nozzle that there had been an increase in CAPTCHAs on its iPhone searches, going up from approximately 19% of total requests to approximately 90%. Thirty-one percent of a sample of blocked attempts from that provider ended up on Google’s sign-in page and the remainder on a CAPTCHA. Searches made from desktop computers were hardly affected, Nozzle says.

    The sign-in page demonstrates “Sign in to continue” with the line “Sign in to verify you’re a human and see more results.” The sign-in button does not link to the search results, according to Nozzle.

    Here’s what the prompt looked like in Clark’s incognito window.

    On Nov. 16, Brodie Clark, who runs SERPalerts, posted a video from an incognito window showing that prior to seeing any results, the user had to enter their credentials.

    The following day, Patel responded to Clark’s post.

    Looking into this. I don’t believe it’s meant to happen on the first page of results like this but we may be testing something here….

    In a recent development, nozzle’s requests also encountered CAPTCHAs and a delay page. From Perkins’s perspective, a CAPTCHA can be solved and the delay waited out, but neither option works on the sign-in wall.

    According to recent reports, the wall adds to the goto link limits I covered on Nov. 5, which cap how fast tools can follow the result links on one Google results page.

    Recent findings suggest that the time period of Nozzle’s 10-hour fall in collection coincided with the time frame during which Google’s November core revision, which started Nov. 10, was still being rolled out. According to Google’s dashboard, the rollout “may take up to 2 weeks to complete” and there were no entries indicating completion when I reviewed the page on Nov. 22.

    Recent findings suggest that prior to reporting a Nov. 18 ranking drop as part of the core revision, first verify whether your rank tracker pulled regular Google search results that day, beginning with mobile. When a drop coincides with a core update, follow Google’s instructions by using Search Console, waiting at least one full week beyond the time when the rollout is finished and then trying a comparison of that week with the week prior to its start.

    Google’s dashboard will show the end date once the core upgrade is complete.

    The sign-in page didn’t go away when Nozzle’s drop ended. It still appeared on a little under 1% of page loads at the provider that reported the iPhone CAPTCHAs, according to Nozzle’s Derek Perkins.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Camunda is the enterprise platform for agentic orchestration, enabling organizations to coordinate AI agents, people, and systems across complex, end-to-end business processes. With built-in governance, auditability, and human oversight, Camunda gives enterprises the control they need to move AI from pilots to production — safely and at scale. Trusted by over 700 organizations worldwide, including 9 of top 10 US banks, Camunda helps enterprises boost operational efficiency, accelerate time-to-value, and deliver better customer experiences.Fully remote and global, we are in the middle of something bigger: transforming into an AI-first organisation, built on our own platform. We use Agentic AI to automate, orchestrate intelligent processes, and elevate human contribution across every team.Named GP Bullhound’s Top 100 Next Unicorn list, 2025 Great Place to Work certified. Visionary in 2025 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Business Orchestration and Automation Technologies. ranked 3rd in Flexa's 2026 Most Flexible Companies, We’re growing fast and looking for top talent to join our team. If you want meaningful work, visible impact and put something genuinely rare on your CV, keep reading.

    In a recent development, camunda Hub is where enterprises run Camunda at scale. From Hub they manage their clusters and tenants, decide who can do what, and roll changes out across the whole organization. We’re looking for a Senior Product Builder to own the backend and architecture that let Hub manage a whole fleet of clusters. Your first focus will be the mechanism that sends access, secret, tenant and licence changes out to every connected cluster and brings deployments, health and audit records back. From there, you’ll shape Hub’s foundations: its event model, the service boundaries and data model other teams build on, and how Hub behaves when things fail or get upgraded. The platform is your product. Your consumers are platform administrators, Centres of Excellence and the builders across Camunda who depend on what you create. You’ll join a latest two-person pod in our remote-first team. You’ll have real ownership as the person who makes the call, and you’ll build AI-first, from written specs through to production. Our customers run mission-critical processes on Camunda, so your work will matter to them every day.

    Take over Hub's fleet propagation mechanism from the team building its first version, and make it work for access, secrets, tenants, licences and custom roles.

    Write short design documents for foundational changes, get them reviewed by the teams that depend on them, and turn them into tested, shipped code.

    Design how Hub behaves when things go wrong: offline clusters, partial failures, Hub outages, and clusters being adopted or detached.

    Build the path from clusters back to Hub, starting with deployment inventory, health, audit records and licence status.

    Design Hub's first event and webhook mechanism, so admins and agents can react to changes instead of polling for them.

    Join the pod's rotations and Hub on-call, and help other builders take on backend work through reviews, guidelines and contract tests.

    What You Will Bring to the Role:.

    Experience building and running backend systems in production that other teams or customers depend on.

    Comfort taking a problem nobody owns yet and turning it into a design, a proposal and shipped code.

    Product judgment for technical consumers: you talk to the people who use your APIs and make trade-offs on their behalf.

    Clear, short writing that lets a remote team review and decide asynchronously.

    Care for how a system behaves when parts of it fail, not only for the happy path.

    Designed and shipped a control plane or similar system that pushes desired state to many targets. Knows outbox or event-log patterns, idempotent apply, versioning, retries and drift reconciliation.

    Senior backend engineering in Java (API design, relational data models, multi-tenant SaaS services) and hands-on Helm and Kubernetes for self-managed installations.

    It has been revealed that software architecture and failure analysis: partial failure, blast radius, consistency trade-offs. Has debugged production incidents in a distributed system and is ready for on-call.

    Industry observers note that has shaped an API or platform as a product, and writes design docs other teams can build on. Gets agreement across teams without formal authority.

    Builds AI-first from written specifications and checks AI output as carefully as any other code.

    Kubernetes operators or GitOps tools, for example Argo CD.

    OIDC, SCIM and permission models, or secret managers and licence systems.

    Camunda 8 or another workflow or orchestration engine.

    Enough frontend skill to build a thin UI on top of a backend capability.

    This role is an existing vacancy.

    35 AI Prompts & Examples For SEO (Updated November 2026) via @sejournal, @theshelleywalsh

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3502 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that good prompting is what makes AI and LLMs valuable for SEO work, from analysis to reporting.
    • Many SEOs have already been prompting for the last few years, but there are so many ways that AI can help; having examples can give us the inspiration to adapt and make this our own.
    • Apart from the right prompts, the one thing an LLM needs is data.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that good prompting is what makes AI and LLMs valuable for SEO work, from analysis to reporting. At Search Engine Journal, the team experiments with AI to wrangle data, handle repetitive tasks, and do deep analysis.

    Many SEOs have already been prompting for the last few years, but there are so many ways that AI can help; having examples can give us the inspiration to adapt and make this our own.

    Apart from the right prompts, the one thing an LLM needs is data. For analysis and reporting, SEO tools can provide the keyword estimates, backlink records, clicks, impressions, and performance data that an LLM doesn’t have. Connect those to ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini and, with the right prompts and some prodding, you can ask more complex questions. For example, which pages have conflicting canonicals, serve a valuable product category, and can be fixed without a template rebuild?

    The following list of 35 prompts covers a range of SEO applications. Many of them need a data connection or an export, and they are designed to take your prompting beyond the basics.

    Use this guide as a basis to experiment, adapt to your own needs and clients, and build your own SEO prompt library.

    Before you copy and run a prompt from this list, read the setup guidance below.

    According to recent reports, the tools an AI needs depend on the work. For a copy review, provide the text and your requirements. For analysis, provide the data. For current research or private SEO data, make sure the AI can access the relevant sources.

    After analysis, check that the results cover the intended data and that important calculations are sound.

    Available tools depend on the account and workspace. So check the current documentation for ChatGPT files, Claude file creation, and Gemini file analysis.

    It has been revealed that for connected SEO data, follow the provider’s setup instructions. Check subscription, API allowance, and dataset requirements, and set a retrieval limit when API usage is charged.

    An effective prompt gives an LLM a clear task, useful context, and specific constraints. When you ask it to work with evidence, add the instruction below to whichever prompt you use:.

    According to recent reports, use customer research to identify the tasks and needs behind people’s questions. The prompt turns those needs into potential search queries, while keeping evidence from customers separate from ideas that still need validation.

    Industry observers note that you need: Customer research, a seed topic, and a clear picture of your audience. Text analysis is enough to map needs; add a keyword export or SEO connector if you also want demand estimates.

    Use a topic and audience to generate distinct questions that could help readers complete a task. The prompt separates questions found in your data from research hypotheses, then recommends which belong in an existing article, a separate resource, or neither.

    Read more about query fan-out for background on this topic and note that Google’s current AI search guidance cautions against creating pages for every possible query variation.

    It has been revealed that an optional source is the Bing AI Performance report. Its sampled grounding queries show retrieval phrases associated with cited content, but they are not necessarily user prompts and do not reveal Google’s fan-out queries.

    Sources indicate that you need: A topic, an audience, and your existing content. Query data can help validate ideas, but you don’t need a specialist connector to generate them.

    Recent findings suggest that check whether an article answers the relevant questions your audience has. The prompt identifies meaningful gaps and proposes only the changes needed to address them, while flagging facts that need research or expert input. Use this template to assess query coverage. If the matter is how the content explains or presents its information, use the content enhancement prompt instead.

    Industry observers note that you need: The article, the reader’s goal, and a list of observed or proposed queries. Include sources for any facts the revision needs.

    Group keywords by search intent and identify which existing or potential page could serve each group. The prompt checks the data before using it and treats overlapping page targets as candidates for review, not proof of cannibalization.

    Industry observers note that you need: A keyword export with metric definitions and a page inventory. Upload the export for data analysis, or use an authorized SEO connector to retrieve equivalent data.

    Recent findings suggest that for prompts that need to inspect live webpages, an Exa or Firecrawl integration can help retrieve page content. For Google ranking data, use a SERP API or supported connector, such as Ahrefs, DataForSEO, or SerpApi.

    Automated Google searches can return results that look plausible but differ from those a person sees in a normal search. SEJ’s report on SERP poisoning explains the issue. Some providers offer safeguards to detect or resolve misleading results. These can reduce errors, but they cannot guarantee accurate results.

    Recent findings suggest that dataForSEO’s resolve_poisoned_results option is off by default. When enabled, it detects and resolves poisoned results and adds the cost of one SERP page to the task.

    Recent findings suggest that keep the search engine, location, language, and device settings consistent, and record when each result set was collected. To compare ranking changes, use two snapshots collected with matching settings. If you do not have a live connector, use dated SERP exports.

    According to recent reports, compare two ranking snapshots to show which queries and pages moved, appeared, or disappeared. The prompt separates observed changes from possible explanations and identifies what evidence would help explain them.

    In a recent development, you need: Two dated rank-tracker or SERP exports collected with matching settings for search engine, market, device, and ranking convention, plus a log of relevant site changes between the two dates. File analysis is enough to compare them.

    In a recent development, review the pages ranking for a query to understand the needs, audiences, and decision stages they serve. The prompt uses that evidence to recommend a purpose and format for your page without treating common SERP patterns as proven ranking factors.

    In a recent development, use this before deciding what a page should do. Choose the content comparison template when you already have a page to audit against the results.

    According to recent reports, you need: A dated SERP sample, accessible result pages, and a brief or draft of your proposed page. The AI needs web access to review the result pages.

    Sources indicate that generate title options that match the page’s search intent and accurately reflect its content. Each option is tied to a reader need and a supporting passage, so you can check that the title’s promise is supported. Use character count as an editing guide, not a fixed Google limit, as Google may shorten displayed titles to fit the available width.

    Industry observers note that use this prompt for title alternatives. Choose the metadata review when you need to diagnose existing titles and descriptions and plan how to evaluate changes.

    In a recent development, you need: The page content, its target search intent, and your brand rules. No plugin is needed.

    Decide whether a page needs an patch, a clearer focus, a separate page, consolidation review, or no change. The prompt checks time-sensitive claims and uses the site inventory, search intent, performance data, and business goal to explain its recommendation.

    You need: The current page, a site inventory, dated search-performance data, and the business goal. Use web research to check claims that may have changed.

    Review whether the content gives readers enough evidence to assess its claims, authorship, methods, and sources. The prompt identifies what is already supported, what is missing, and what needs to be verified without inventing experience or credentials.

    You need: The content and verified information about its author, organization, methods, and sources.

    Build a year-long plan that connects content ideas to reader needs and business objectives. This prompt checks existing coverage, seasonality, launch dates, and team capacity, while keeping later plans provisional where evidence is limited.

    Sources indicate that you need: Keyword or trend data, launch dates, an existing content inventory, and production capacity. Enable file creation to produce a spreadsheet. A calendar connector is optional if you provide the dates.

    According to recent reports, assess whether pages should stay separate, be differentiated, updated, or consolidated. The prompt weighs duplicated information against distinct reader needs and outlines what to preserve if a merge is recommended.

    Industry observers note that you need: The candidate pages, crawl and internal-link data, query-to-page performance, and relevant backlink data. Uploaded exports are enough for data analysis.

    It has been revealed that review a draft for factual accuracy, sourcing, attribution, contradictions, and clear style issues. The prompt also flags generic sections that need stronger evidence or examples, without claiming to certify originality or authorship.

    In a recent development, you need: The draft, your house style, sources, and any material for comparison. Use web access to check missing or current factual references.

    According to recent reports, study a defined sample of competitor pages to understand the topics, formats, and evidence they use. The prompt identifies strategic options based on that sample without assuming it reveals the competitor’s full strategy or performance.

    Use this to study publishing patterns and strategic choices. Choose coverage gaps when you need a prioritized list of unmet reader needs from two content inventories.

    Recent findings suggest that you need: Competitor content inventories, your own content or assets, and a limit on the research. Use browsing or a bounded crawl; performance comparisons require actual data.

    Compare your page with a defined set of ranking pages using a dated SERP export or provider dataset. This prompt looks at reader needs, evidence, examples, and decision support, then identifies where your page can improve or contribute something different.

    You need: The keyword, market, device, a dated SERP export, and your content. An authorized provider connection can supply the export; ordinary web search cannot replace a ranking snapshot.

    Find places where a link would help readers, using only the destinations you supply. Each recommendation includes the existing anchor text and a reason for the link, with questionable or unsuitable URLs flagged for checking.

    Industry observers note that you need: The source article and a current destination list with URLs, summaries, and status. No connector is needed if you provide these.

    Review whether the title and description match the page and its search intent. Suggest alternatives based on the content, then outline how to assess any change using comparable data without assuming it will improve click-through rate.

    You need: The current metadata, page content, a comparable SERP sample, and optional query performance data. Text analysis is enough.

    Identify specific explanations, evidence, or visuals that would make the page more useful. Recommend additions only when they address a reader’s need, and flag any research or assets still required.

    Industry observers note that you need: The content, the reader’s task, available assets, and relevant data. Image or chart tools are optional if you want approved additions produced.

    Use screenshots to review the page’s visible layout and messaging, then suggest tests for potential improvements. Keep visual observations separate from hypotheses about behavior, speed, or functionality.

    According to recent reports, you need: Desktop and mobile screenshots, the page content, and the conversion goal. Include funnel or performance data to assess visitor behavior or page speed.

    It has been revealed that assess whether each location has enough distinct customer need and verified information to justify its own page. For locations that qualify, draft relevant copy and flag local details that still need confirmation.

    Recent findings suggest that you need: Confirmed service areas, local business facts, offers, and supporting evidence. Use web research to check current local sources.

    According to recent reports, turn real customer questions into concise answers based on approved business information. Check current local rules against official sources and flag questions that need a business decision or further verification.

    According to recent reports, you need: Actual customer questions, approved business information, and current official sources for local rules. No FAQ plugin is needed to draft answers.

    According to recent reports, use backlink data to find relevant pages that may have a reason to reference your work. Check the source pages and your assets before drafting specific outreach – the recommendations are not guaranteed placements, and no messages are sent.

    You need: A backlink gap export or authorized SEO provider connection, your relevant assets, and web research access. Set a maximum number of pages to inspect.

    Compare your content with a competitor’s to find reader needs your pages may not serve. Prioritize possible gaps using business relevance and any demand data you provide, rather than assuming a competitor’s topic proves demand.

    It has been revealed that you need: Your content inventory, a competitor’s inventory, and readable pages. Add keyword or performance data for quantitative prioritization.

    In a recent development, turn SEO evidence into either an analytical report or a one-page executive memo. Calculate from raw data when needed, explain what the evidence supports, and make ROI claims only when the value and cost basis are agreed.

    According to recent reports, you need: Search and analytics exports or checked performance metrics, source definitions, comparable periods, business goals, and a change log. Include costs and an agreed value basis if you want an ROI calculation. Use data analysis for calculations – text analysis is enough to summarize checked findings.

    Compare crawl, sitemap, and URL Inspection evidence to investigate why crucial pages are missing from search or have a different selected canonical. The results identify issues and checks to follow; they do not guarantee indexing or make site changes. The URL Inspection API reports on Google’s indexed version. It does not run a live URL test.

    In a recent development, you need: A crawl export, sitemap, priority pages, and URL Inspection results or a documented inspection sample. A normal crawl can show declared canonicals, but not Google’s selected canonical.

    Sources indicate that compare the server HTML with the rendered page to find differences in content, links, directives, and structured data. Treat those differences as evidence to investigate, not proof of what every crawler can access.

    In a recent development, you need: Server HTML, rendered HTML, response headers, and a screenshot for the same URL. Add Google’s rendered-page evidence if available.

    Recent findings suggest that use Chrome DevTools MCP to inspect slow form and CTA interactions. Check whether analytics, tag-manager callbacks, or other scripts contribute to delays rather than assuming tracking is the cause.

    Recent findings suggest that you need: An approved test page, representative interactions, known tracking scripts, and an AI client that supports MCP servers with Chrome DevTools MCP connected, such as a coding agent. The standard ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini chat apps cannot run this prompt unless that connection is set up. Add field INP data where available. A controlled trace diagnoses tested interactions, not every real user’s page experience.

    According to recent reports, chrome DevTools MCP’s performance tools may send the URLs you trace to Google’s CrUX API to fetch real-user field data. If your test URLs are confidential, check the documentation for how to turn this off before you run a trace.

    See Google’s INP guidance for the metric and the official Chrome DevTools MCP documentation for browser and performance tools.

    In a recent development, check whether existing structured data matches the visible page and verified facts. Google’s structured data policies require markup to reflect visible content, so identify unsupported or conflicting properties and suggest the smallest change needed, without promising rich results or AI citations.

    You need: Existing JSON-LD, visible page content, verified business or product facts, and any validation results. Web access helps check current requirements.

    Industry observers note that turn technical audit findings into a prioritized work queue. Group related issues, explain their business relevance and dependencies, and distinguish confirmed defects from warnings that still need investigation.

    You need: A technical audit or crawl export, affected URLs, business priorities, and any available performance data. Include engineering estimates only if your team has supplied them.

    Compare your intended access policy with crawler rules, headers, firewall controls, logs, and Search Console settings. Separate search, training, user-request, and ad-validation access, then recommend changes and checks without applying them.

    You need: Your intended access policy, robots.txt, response headers, relevant CDN or firewall rules, sampled server logs, and the current Search Console generative AI setting, including inherited settings.

    Compare saved AI answers across comparable runs, keeping brand mentions, recommendations, and linked citations distinct. Report counts and rates with clear denominators, and treat changes in a limited sample as observations rather than universal visibility trends.

    Industry observers note that you need: Saved AI answers and cited URLs, with prompts, dates, platform, locale, and available model or session details. A monitoring service is optional if it provides those fields.

    Industry observers note that compare AI search impressions, search clicks, AI referrals, and key events while keeping each source and metric separate. Check changes in tracking and reporting, and avoid attributing visits or conversions to citations when the data cannot establish that link.

    Recent findings suggest that you need: Search Console performance exports, analytics referral and key-event data, and optional Bing AI Performance exports. Include channel definitions and tracking changes.

    Check what the assistant actually received before interpreting it. Review scope, fields, row counts, missing values, duplicates, metric definitions, and joins, then report what the data can and cannot support.

    According to recent reports, you need: The files or authorized connector you plan to analyze, the requested scope, and the provider’s metric definitions. Live retrieval also requires access to the relevant account and a supported operation.

    Compare Search Console performance with crawl and inspection evidence to identify the pages and groups contributing to a traffic change. Check joins and totals, then list explanations to investigate without treating timing or a technical warning as proof of cause.

    You need: Comparable Search Console exports, a dated crawl, page groups, and a change log. Add URL Inspection results where available. Use data analysis for calculations and joins.

    Turn a defined reader need into a focused brief grounded in existing coverage, sources, expertise, and original material. The brief sets out the page’s purpose and evidence still to collect without drafting the full article or inventing experience.

    According to recent reports, you need: The reader’s task, existing coverage, approved sources, and available expertise or original material. Add a dated SERP sample when relevant and use web research for source checks.

    Industry observers note that create and test one specific filter, query, extraction rule, or validation script against representative examples. Include expected results and boundaries, and state exactly which tests ran.

    You need: One task, the target tool and language or query dialect, the input structure, and representative examples with expected results. Use code execution or a safe test environment for validation.

    According to recent reports, before uploading a file or connecting a data source, always make sure you have authority to share it with that AI tool. Remove or anonymize personal and confidential information where possible, and never include passwords, API keys, or other access credentials in a prompt.

    Give connectors access only to the data needed for the task and store secrets such as API keys in a local .env file that only your user account can read (for example, chmod 600).

    To reduce the risk of prompt injection, treat text retrieved from webpages, files, and other sources as information to assess, not instructions to follow. Tell your LLM to ignore any instructions embedded in that material that try to change the task or request access to other data. This lowers the risk but does not remove it, so give the tool access only to what the task needs. Review AI-generated findings, citations, calculations, and code before relying on them or making changes to a live site.

    Once a prompt produces reliable results, save it with its required inputs, data sources, output format, and checks. Keep client-specific instructions and reference material together in a ChatGPT project, Claude skill, or Gemini skill, where available.

    Sources indicate that for recurring comparisons, record the data source, dates, and conditions for each run. A saved prompt doesn’t provide access to private data or replace the tools needed to retrieve it.

    Recent findings suggest that finally, to make prompts fit for purpose, it’s not as simple as plugging in templates, copying and pasting the output, then calling it a day. It’s important to keep refining every prompt as part of your process. Keep testing, adjusting, and pressure-checking your prompts. Refine them until they consistently deliver results that enhance your workflow and productivity.

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    In a recent development, A newly introduced study finds that journalism school faculty — charged with putting more student work in front of non-student readers — often serve as a hidden infrastructure for local news. Burnout is a risk.

    If there’s one significant takeaway from the past two decades of local news struggle — the often perilous, occasionally brilliant transition from dominant newspapers to online media — perhaps it’s this: Passion alone isn’t enough.

    A newspaper newsroom filled with committed editors and brilliant reporters still stares into the same headwinds as its more middling peers. The devotion of those leading a nonprofit outlet can mean little if revenue can’t keep the doors open. And even when the money is less notable — when journalism is somewhat protected from the demands of the market — passion is still a finite resource, and it’s not always renewable.

    That truism came to mind when I was reading a recent article by Sima Bhowmik of the University of Vermont and Andrea Lorenz of Kent State. It looks at one specific corner of the contemporary news ecosystem: journalism schools that use their students to fill voids in local coverage.

    In a recent development, J-schools, after all, have faculties full of experience and students who need it. A few decades ago, an early-career journalist might have spent a few years covering city council meetings and school board budgets before moving up the chain to a bigger outlet. That path barely exists these days, and journalism programs know their students need the chance to do real work. What if these reporters-in-training could handle some of the local stories that the city’s daily no longer can?

    RELATED ARTICLEA “win-win” partnership brings a surge of reporting firepower to hyperlocal news outlets around BostonSarah ScireNovember 13, 2025RELATED ARTICLELen Downie: The teaching hospital model works, but it will require drastic changeLeonard Downie Jr.September 12, 2012If you happen to live near a college with a journalism program, you’ve probably seen this idea — often called the “teaching hospital” model — in action. Here in the Boston suburbs, many of the stories I read about my town are written by Boston University students. According to UVM’s Center for Community News, where Bhowmik is an assistant research professor, there were 282 such efforts as of 2025, producing local news inside 205 colleges and universities. Those numbers were up from 227 programs in 172 colleges the year before — a boom fueled by a surge in philanthropic funding for these partnerships.

    Bhowmik and Lorentz’s paper — published in Journalism & Mass Communication Educator — is the result of interviews with 118 faculty and staff at 101 of those colleges, and their major takeaway is one that will be familiar to many in local news: They’re exhausted.

    It has been revealed that participants repeatedly used phrases such as “at capacity,” “don’t have the bandwidth,” “not enough hours of the day,” and “it’s just a lot” to describe the workload. Several described long workdays and exhaustion, with one participant saying the amount of editing “just about kills me every semester.” At many institutions, faculty workload was intensified by staffing shortages, retirements, hiring freezes, and budget cuts. This left faculty with little time to provide the one-on-one coaching necessary to elevate student stories to publishable quality… “What’s happening in the academic ecosystem is so phenomenal, thanks to these really passionate founders on the faculty,” Bhowmik told me. “But the extra work they’re putting it isn’t always getting acknowledged within the system. A professor might be editing 10 or 20 stories a week, by students without much experience, on top of a full teaching load. There’s a lot of overwork and some dissatisfaction, even though they know how key the work is.” (See above: Passion alone isn’t enough.) Here’s how one faculty member described their situation: Think about it: Like, how many reporters does the average assigning editor at a mid-sized newspaper supervise? Half a dozen? So try, like, 20 of them, and each of them is writing for a different outlet maybe, which has its own set of deadlines and editor. And they’re all at varying skill levels, and broadly, they’re all pretty new. Their copy requires a lot of work, their reporting often requires a lot of handholding. Another talked about the responsibility of getting student work up to the level a news outlet expects. You can’t just give a meh student story a C- and be done with it if a local editor is expecting publishable copy. It takes a lot of work to get student work up to the quality of professionally published work. And a lot of students start out with really good ideas, do some good reporting by the time they’re done in the semester, it needs work, and that tends to fall on the faculty person. And that’s a lot of work outside of uncompensated work…But bridging that gap between what a student produces at the end of a semester and what can actually be published is still a big gap that needs to be addressed. And aside from the editing work, faculty described the administrative burden of being the connective tissue joining two distinct worlds. Negotiating pitches, coordinating deadlines, dealing with revisions, shepherding copy flows — all of it with students who are juggling other courses, work-study jobs, and the life of college student — can be “difficult to sustain without administrative support, dedicated staff, or funding for editors,” they write. Just to save a few dozen proud Mizzou alums from emailing me: Yes, the “teaching hospital” model is not a new idea. The idea of giving journalism students real-world experience in public-facing outlets has been central to the Missouri Method for more than a century, and other major journalism schools have long done versions of this work. But Bhowmik notes that many of these new efforts are in smaller colleges with smaller journalism programs — places without the in-house infrastructure of a Columbia Missourian or KOMU, where media partnerships involve more ongoing negotiation. That can leave more of the pressure of sustainability on one or two overworked faculty members. As Bhowmik and Lorenz put it: …faculty labor is not incidental to the model; it is the hidden infrastructure that allows student work to move from classroom assignment to public-facing journalism. We argue that passion may help launch these programs, but passion alone is not a sustainable staffing model. If universities treat these initiatives as ordinary courses while expecting faculty to function simultaneously as instructors, editors, partnership managers, and newsroom supervisors, the model remains vulnerable to burnout and institutional instability. None of this, of course, is to say that these academic-publisher partnerships aren’t performing valuable roles in hundreds of communities. These programs have generated thousands of stories that otherwise might never have reached the public. But the sort of exhaustion Bhowmik and Lorenz describe reminds me a lot of what we saw in the first wave of local nonprofit news outlets in the late 2000s and early 2010s. Many of those were founded by idealistic journalists — often refugees from the local daily — who saw the opportunity to do something new and valuable for their communities. They put in long hours editing stories, selling ads, pitching foundations, and building audiences. And within a few years, a lot of them were burnt out, and their outlets suffered for it. In the decade-plus since, funders have gotten smarter about building institutional capacity — knowing that passion can only fuel so much. The world Bhowmik and Lorenz describe inside these journalism programs makes me think that department chairs and deans would be wise to consider a similar pivot to make these academic-publisher partnerships sustainable for the long term.

    “What’s happening in the academic ecosystem is so phenomenal, thanks to these really passionate founders on the faculty,” Bhowmik told me. “But the extra work they’re putting it isn’t always getting acknowledged within the system. A professor might be editing 10 or 20 stories a week, by students without much experience, on top of a full teaching load. There’s a lot of overwork and some dissatisfaction, even though they know how important the work is.”.

    In a recent development, canada’s proposed federal budget includes some good news for local journalism. The federal government is extending its journalism tax credit by $501 million, expanding eligibility to audio and audiovisual news organizations, and renewing the Local Journalism Initiative, which supports journalism in underserved communities.

    RELATED ARTICLEIn Canada, a government program to support local news tries to determine who’s most deservingSarah ScireMay 8, 2020Sarah wrote about the Local Journalism Initiative in its early days. A study earlier this year found that reporters paid with LJI funding believed they maintained their roles as watchdogs and wrote balanced stories, though two-thirds of interviewees were concerned about the perception of a conflict of interest. A growing number of journalists say the benefits of government subsidies for journalism outweigh the drawbacks.

    Sources indicate that A recent report in The Tyee suggests government support is essential to the survival of local media in Canada. (The Tyee has received support from the Local Journalism Initiative.).

    It has been revealed that “It’s either this or death, frankly,” LJI program director and Canadian Association of Journalists president Brent Jolly told The Tyee. “It’s not about local news editors getting their marching orders from the Prime Minister’s Office like some conspiracy theorists want you to think. It’s about infrastructure.”.

    Lisa Sygutek, publisher of the Crowsnest Pass Herald in Alberta, credited the LJI with growing the publication from “a 16-page paper to a 24-page paper.”.

    Read more in The Tyee’s look at Canadian local news here.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that google published latest guidance on how to keep from blocking its user-triggered AI agents that identify themselves as Google-Agent.
    • It has been revealed that google’s latest guidance on Google-Agent may be related to its announcement of the expansion of Personal Intelligence, which came after this article was originally published.
    • Personal Intelligence enables Google to draw on information from across its products and services to better understand what users want to accomplish and provide increasingly personalized assistance.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that google published latest guidance on how to keep from blocking its user-triggered AI agents that identify themselves as Google-Agent. The new documentation shows how to verify legitimate Google-Agent requests and configure firewalls to allow them on websites.

    It has been revealed that google’s latest guidance on Google-Agent may be related to its announcement of the expansion of Personal Intelligence, which came after this article was originally published. Both developments are consistent with Google CEO Sundar Pichai’s description of a unified experience across Google’s products and services that’s mediated by an agentic layer.

    Personal Intelligence enables Google to draw on information from across its products and services to better understand what users want to accomplish and provide increasingly personalized assistance.

    Google’s announcement offers an example of how this works:.

    “So if you’ve been researching and planning for a trip, you can pick up right where you left off in a fresh search thread without starting over or repeating yourself.”.

    Industry observers note that planning a trip can involve researching destinations, comparing accommodations, and making reservations. That’s precisely the kind of task-based search where user-triggered AI agents may fetch information from websites, interact with them, and complete tasks on behalf of users.

    What makes the timing of Google’s Google-Agent guidance interesting is that Google is simultaneously expanding its ability to understand what users want to accomplish and publishing guidance for website owners on how to make sure that user-triggered AI agents are not blocked from accessing websites.

    Although Google has not explicitly connected Google-Agent to Personal Intelligence, the two developments appear to complement each other in terms of Google’s larger goal of creating a personalized, task-based Search experience.

    Google-Agent is the name used by AI agents hosted on Google’s infrastructure that navigate websites and perform actions on behalf of users. Google’s guidance and also Google’s User-Triggered Fetcher documentation do not identify which Google products or services use Google-Agent. Neither documentation mentions Google Search, AI Mode, Gemini, or any other Google product.

    It describes Google-Agent as agents that are hosted on Google’s infrastructure, interact with and navigate websites, and complete tasks on behalf of a user.

    The document says or implies that the Google-Agent does the following:.

    The new guidance explains there are three ways that website owners can verify that a request comes from Google-Agent.

    1. The request’s User-Agent header contains “Google-Agent.”.

    It has been revealed that 2. The request originates from an IP address listed in Google’s published file of user-triggered agent ranges.

    3. Only where it’s present, when the request carries a cryptographic signature under Google’s experimental Web Bot Auth protocol, which can be checked against Google’s published public keys.

    The first two checks are the baseline, and the signature check adds stronger verification when it’s available. A Google-Agent bot can then be allowed through whatever bot defenses are in use once it passes those checks. Google also notes that some CDNs and bot-detection services handle this verification automatically.

    Lastly, Google offers guidance on troubleshooting when the Google-Agent is unintentionally blocked.

    Google recommends ensuring that rules allowing Google-Agent requests have higher priority and are evaluated before broader blocking rules, including:.

    If bot detection, firewall (WAF), or CDN rules only covers the initial page request, the agent will be able to land on the website but it will be unable to finish whatever task it’s there to accomplish.

    Google recommends checking that CAPTCHA challenges are disabled for verified Google-Agent requests, reviewing rate limits, IP address updates, and proxy configurations.

    “Proxy headers: Confirm that load balancers and intermediate proxies preserve the original client IP, the User-Agent header, and (for signed requests) the Signature, Signature-Input, and Signature-Agent headers.”.

    Google’s new guidance addresses three complications to check if Google-Agent is being inadvertently blocked:.

    “Shared-IP rate limits: Confirm that per-IP rate-limiting rules account for or exempt verified Google-Agent IP ranges, as concurrent requests from multiple consumers share the same egress pool.

    IP range updates: Confirm that IP-based rules stay synced with the latest ranges in user-triggered-agents.json.

    Proxy headers: Confirm that load balancers and intermediate proxies preserve the original client IP, the User-Agent header, and (for signed requests) the Signature, Signature-Input, and Signature-Agent headers.”.

    Google’s new Google-Agent guidance offers tips for website owners who want to allow Google-Agent interactions, stressing that they need to make sure that legitimate Google-Agent requests can pass through security defenses without compromising protections against unwanted bots.

    📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1678 w)

    Breaking: AI is becoming an information gateway. Audiences still don’t want it making their news.

    📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1678 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • Sources indicate that we will never sell your address.
    • According to recent reports, we have sent a confirmation link to .
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    Sources indicate that we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    According to recent reports, we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries said they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary.

    In my Nieman Lab prediction this time last year, I wrote that “in 2026, the use of AI as an information gateway will only rise further.”.

    As it turns out, I was right. In fresh research that I published with my colleagues Rasmus Kleis Nielsen and Richard Fletcher, one of our many findings is that generative AI systems are becoming ever more significant information intermediaries, both when intentionally used and when incidentally encountered.

    It has been revealed that for our new report, “Generative AI and News Report 2026: From Standalone Tools to Information Infrastructure,”  we surveyed audiences across nine countries, including the United States, on their use of AI in their everyday lives, what they think its impact will be on different sectors of society, and what they think about its use in news and journalism specifically. I obviously think you should read the whole report, but here are some of the major takeaways.

    Industry observers note that the use of standalone conversational AI systems such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini continues to grow rapidly, with 51% of respondents across the six countries where we have past data saying they now use AI weekly (49% in the U.S.). That’s a faster spread, at least in the U.S., than smartphones or the internet saw.

    Many people also encounter AI through “incidental” AI exposure in the AI-infused services and platforms they’re already using. Search engines such as Google and Bing are key drivers: 57% of respondents across countries said they saw or engaged with AI-generated answers or summaries in the last week. News media, too, drives AI exposure. An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries said they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary.

    Recent findings suggest that despite all the talk about AI agents, we find that, so far, they haven’t broken into the mainstream. The vast majority of respondents across all nine countries (67%) stated they had not used an AI agent in the last week. Fourteen percent used one for a real task and 13% tried one just to experiment.

    Industry observers note that our data provides solid evidence that a broader transformation of the information environment is afoot. Conversational AI systems have arrived as information intermediaries. Trust is not the main reason people use them. Instead, people see conversational AI systems as friction-reducing machines that get them information more quickly.

    In a recent development, “Getting information” continues to be the most common use case. Thirty-eight percent of respondents across countries (35% in the U.S.) said they had used generative AI for getting information in the last week, up from 24% in 2025 and 11% in 2024.

    Sources indicate that we looked more closely at what people do when they say they use AI for getting information. Across the six countries we’ve surveyed since 2024, we primarily see a mixture of search-equivalent behaviors like “researching a topic” (24%) or “answering factual questions” (18%). People are also increasingly turning to AI for advice (20%).

    Sources indicate that using AI directly for news, meanwhile, remains a niche activity, as we demonstrated in the Digital News Report earlier this year. But that use is increasing: 9% of respondents across our six core countries say they use AI for news, up from 6% in 2025 and 3% in 2024.

    It has been revealed that many people don’t hold clear or strong views about whether AI output is trustworthy. But people who do rely on it for information trust it. Across the nine countries, 75% of those who used AI to answer factual questions trusted the answers, as did 76% of those who used it for advice and 72% of those who used it for news. Only small minorities expressed distrust.

    Sources indicate that at the same time, trust and trustworthiness do not, at this stage, seem to be central to why people rely on AI systems. Instead, people tend to see these systems as friction-reducing machines. The convenience of getting a faster and easier answer was chosen by 64% as the main reason they use AI, followed by the interactivity afforded by natural language interfaces (56%). Only a minority (21%) noted they use AI because they get more reliable information from it than from other sources.

    As AI systems become widely used, their growing popularity is likely to affect the use of legacy content offerings and digital platforms and services. As my coauthor Rasmus Kleis Nielsen put it on LinkedIn, rapid growth in AI use isn’t just eating into what news sites have to offer. It’s eating into search, too — with people who use AI for information saying they use not just news, but search engines less, too, and by a wider margin. Challenging times may be ahead not just for news publishers, but also for the incumbent digital giants previously seen as unassailable.

    As in previous years, we wanted to know what people think of AI’s use in journalism and news. We find that people’s attitudes here are remarkably entrenched and negative — though they also haven’t worsened significantly.

    People across countries remain uncomfortable with the use of AI in the newsroom, especially with the idea of news being made entirely or primarily with AI. On average across nine countries, just 12% of respondents say they are very or somewhat comfortable with news made entirely by AI. That figure rises to 19% if there is some human oversight. This has hardly changed since 2024, and the gap between human- and AI-made news appears in every country we surveyed.

    Sources indicate that this also remains true regardless of whether it is breaking news or reporting. People are even more uncomfortable with AI being used for commentary or opinion — formats where the expectation that a human should share their view is strongest.

    Our findings raise several important questions for journalists and publishers navigating the rise of generative AI.

    According to recent reports, first, generative AI is becoming an increasingly significant information intermediaries, with a number of possible knock-on effects on news. People are using AI to reduce friction by getting “good enough” outputs for some information needs — and skipping legacy platforms, established publishers, and the time and effort it takes to find the best available information. Discovery, brand attribution, data collection, and monetization all grow more challenging for publishers in this context.

    Second, even though use continues to grow, the public remains skeptical of AI in news. This isn’t just a challenge for newsrooms’ internal adoption. It also indicates that publishers using AI need to communicate to audiences what’s in it for them.

    It has been revealed that third, beyond news, our findings speak to wider debates about AI’s societal impact. As in other studies on this topic, we find that uptake of AI is uneven. Weekly use is more common among people in professional occupations than those in entry-level or service occupations. Most people rely on free — usually less advanced — AI models.

    The differences in how — not just whether — people use AI may become a upcoming dividing line. As AI researcher and OpenAI cofounder Andrej Karpathy recently argued, there is a widening “gap in shared understanding of LLM capability,” with most people not seeing what has left those inside AI firms both excited and worried.

    According to recent reports, expectations of what AI will do differ far more between daily people and people who have never used it than between any other groups in our survey. When two groups form very different views of the same technology because they have such different starting points, there will likely be consequences.

    Industry observers note that this doesn’t matter just for people’s individual choices around whether and how to make use of AI in their own lives. It also matters where AI is adopted and governed through collective decisions — in public services, for example — that apply to those who do not use it.

    Felix Simon is the research fellow in AI, information, and news at the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism and a research associate at the Oxford Internet Institute (OII) at the University of Oxford.

    The Final Ad Checklist Before BFCM – What To Fix Now & What To Leave via @sejournal, @tonyadam

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2313 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
