    #124957. Ad Tech Briefing: Meta eyes CTV as AppLovin circles Criteo, signs of the squeeze on independent ad tech

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1213 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    Ad Tech Briefing: Meta eyes CTV as AppLovin circles Criteo, signs of the squeeze on independent ad tech

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1213 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that join us Dec.
    • This Ad Tech Briefing covers the latest in ad tech and platforms for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Tuesday at 10 a.m.
    • AppLovin’s reported interest in Criteo and Meta’s prepares to explore CTV could put further pressure on independent ad tech, with some companies reporting challenging circumstances in the latest round of earnings calls.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    This Ad Tech Briefing covers the latest in ad tech and platforms for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Tuesday at 10 a.m. ET. More from the series →.

    AppLovin’s reported interest in Criteo and Meta’s prepares to explore CTV could put further pressure on independent ad tech, with some companies reporting challenging circumstances in the latest round of earnings calls.

    Last week, Reuters reported unconfirmed acquisition discussions involving AppLovin and Criteo, the same day Next in Media reported that Meta was exploring partnerships with television manufacturers and free FAST services to extend its advertising platform into CTV.

    If both sets of developments materialize, it would represent two of the largest established (mobile) ad platforms expanding into new channels using existing advertiser relationships, data, and buying technology.

    It’s well understood that AppLovin wants to extend its performance advertising business beyond mobile applications, and Criteo — a manufacturer that is reportedly seeking an exit from the public markets — could provide retail relationships, commerce data, and access to advertisers across the open web.

    Meanwhile, Meta could use its existing buying platform to help advertisers reach television audiences without relying on a separate demand-side platform.

    In recent weeks, separate sources told Digiday this could prove a key advantage in helping the social networking outfit eat into Google’s lead in markets where its DSP, DV 360, dominates.

    However, developments could reduce advertisers’ dependence on independent DSPs and supply-side platforms.

    AppLovin’s potential shortcut into commerce.

    Private equity firms Vista Equity Partners and Quinti Capital have also reportedly expressed interest in Criteo, which has engaged an investment bank to evaluate its options.

    AppLovin reported third-quarter revenue of $2.19 billion, up 55% year over year, alongside $1.44 billion in net income.

    Criteo reported a 12% revenue decline to $416 million, with net income falling to approximately $6 million.

    AppLovin’s growth has been driven by mobile advertising, although the tech giant is increasingly targeting e-commerce advertisers outside of gaming.

    Criteo has spent years expanding beyond retargeting into commerce media, developing relationships with retailers, access to shopper data and cross-channel advertising capabilities.

    Per official figures, Criteo’s commerce intelligence draws on more than $1 trillion in annual transactions, 740 million daily active users and over 5 billion product SKUs, and acquiring it could accelerate AppLovin’s expansion into retail media, providing relationships and data it would otherwise need to develop independently.

    However, integrating the businesses would be complicated given that AppLovin’s core technology is built around mobile apps, while Criteo operates across retailers, publishers, and other commerce environments.

    The potential benefits would depend on whether their different data assets, buying systems, and commercial relationships could work effectively when integrated.

    Earlier in the year, multiple sources told Digiday that Meta is ⁠exploring an option that would allow advertisers to extend campaigns into third-party television inventory through its existing advertising tools — a measurement tactic commonly known as audience extension.

    The latest reporting suggests Meta is considering how those relationships could support an advertiser-facing buying option, resembling Pinterest’s CTV audience-extension offering, which lets advertisers use Pinterest’s audience data to reach consumers beyond its owned properties. Meta could pursue a similar approach at considerably greater scale.

    Its existing advertiser base could access television inventory without establishing separate relationships with specialist CTV buying platforms, an attractive option for smaller advertisers already using Meta’s automated campaign tools.

    For DSPs and SSPs, the competitive implications would be significant, as Meta could bring more advertisers directly into CTV, potentially reducing the role of intermediaries that connect buyers with television inventory.

    Industry observers note that but questions remain about how the proposed model would operate. For example, would Meta determine which inventory advertisers purchase? Plus, how would fees and media costs be disclosed? And what independent measurement would be available?

    Such details are likely to determine whether Meta’s proposed offering creates a meaningful alternative to existing CTV buying arrangements or simply adds another layer between advertisers and publishers.

    • The retailer is preparing to launch a connector to Muse that will provide the AI agent with defined access to its e-commerce infrastructure, meaning it gets to set the guardrails and boundaries within which Meta’s agent can browse and shop.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    By letting Meta’s Muse agent into its stores only through the gateway it built and controls, Walmart is treating AI agent access the way retail media networks once treated ad slots: as inventory to be doled out on its own terms.

    The retailer is preparing to launch a connector to Muse that will provide the AI agent with defined access to its e-commerce infrastructure, meaning it gets to set the guardrails and boundaries within which Meta’s agent can browse and shop.

    The capability was noticed by Juozas Kaziukėnas, founder of e-commerce research firm Marketplace Pulse, after he spotted an enhancement to Walmart’s technical instruction manual for Muse. According to The Verge, that integration launches tomorrow (Nov. 24), in time for Black Friday Cyber Monday shopping.

    According to recent reports, the manual, which Digiday has also seen and verified, describes how Muse can interact with Walmart’s shopping systems on behalf of a user. This includes tasks like searching for products, answering questions, building shopping carts and, if permission is granted, completing orders. Muse can also call on Walmart’s own shopping assistant Sparky to answer questions about products, stores and comparisons.

    So a Walmart Shopper could ask Muse to compare three televisions, find specific ingredients for a dinner party, or ask the agent to add products to its Walmart shopping cart. Muse can then use Walmart’s systems to carry out those tasks. For example, Walmart could help Muse identify a customer’s usual brand of milk without handing over their entire shopping history.

    In a recent development, this goes beyond what someone might typically expect from a chatbot, where a user might simply ask for recommendations. Instead, Muse, through the gateway to Walmart’s own marketplace, can act on those recommendations, taking care of the legwork involved in shopping and even making purchases once the user has given the necessary permission.

    Walmart talked about its vision for this in its blog post last month.

    It has been revealed that built using the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the integration gives AI agents a more direct and reliable way to interact with Walmart’s shopping systems. It’s designed to let agents shop on a customer’s behalf without giving them access to their wider purchase history or unnecessary personal information. For example, Walmart could help Muse identify a customer’s usual brand of milk without handing over their entire shopping history.

    According to recent reports, walmart has also started introducing Agent Profiles, which gives each AI agent its own dedicated profile within a customer’s Walmart account. It means shoppers can distinguish purchases made by an AI agent from the ones they’ve completed themselves, while deciding how much autonomy they want to give the agent. Customers can require approval for every purchase, or set a spending limit (such as $50, $100 or $200), allowing the agent to spend up to that amount without seeking approval each time. Customers also have the ability to disable the agent’s access at any time.

    Recent findings suggest that this development comes after Amazon already blocked Muse from accessing its e-commerce site in September, arguing that third-party AI agents should operate openly and respect retailers’ decisions about whether to participate. At the time, Amazon said it asked Meta to remove its website from Muse’s shopping experience, but Meta declined. It also raised concerns about Muse accessing customer accounts without authorization and potentially capturing customer credentials. However, Meta disputed the claims, saying Muse cannot see consumers’ passwords or payment details.

    In a recent development, while Walmart might be working closer with Muse going forward, this approach could raise questions about its ad business. In particular, with Muse increasingly allowed to take over product discovery, where does that leave its sponsored product placements and how much influence will brands have over what an AI agent recommends.

    It has been revealed that “There will emerge a new advertising mechanism where brands will pay dollars not for a sponsored placement, but for a ‘sponsored consideration’ to the agents,” said Abhishek Bora, head of digital growth at All Star Elite. “If agents take over the buying process, how would a new brand with a better product and offer get considered by an agent when it has no history of reviews, usage or purchases?”.

    Neither Walmart nor Meta responded to Digiday’s request for comment.

    As Black Friday Cyber Monday rapidly approaches, brands are most focused on acquiring fresh customers this holiday season.

    Product discovery habits are changing, leaving marketers unsure how to pivot ahead of the biggest sales period of the year.

    Amazon is paying to reach ChatGPT shoppers while the chatbot is finding other ways to surface its products and deals.

    Why brands are writing no-AI clauses into creator deals

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (690 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, join us Dec.
    • Influencer marketing contracts have become a focal point in the creator economy.
    • “We actually are seeing more and more contracts including language around the creator not being able to use AI in their content for these campaigns,” said Kurt Stadelman, vp of talent at creator marketing firm Pearpop, in a conversation with Digiday managing editor Sara Jerde during Digiday’s recent Creator Strategies event.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Influencer marketing contracts have become a focal point in the creator economy. There’s heightened attention being paid by brands, creators and creators’ representatives to deal terms, such as usage rights, exclusivity and payment terms. But among the newest addendums is AI usage.

    “We actually are seeing more and more contracts including language around the creator not being able to use AI in their content for these campaigns,” said Kurt Stadelman, vp of talent at creator marketing firm Pearpop, in a conversation with Digiday managing editor Sara Jerde during Digiday’s recent Creator Strategies event.

    It has been revealed that creators are actually welcoming brands’ no-AI demands, he remarked. Creators are already concerned about generative AI being used to create content and crowd out creators from people’s feeds. So brands forbidding AI-generated content from creators signals a commitment by brands to human-made content, said Stadelman.

    According to recent reports, but what counts as AI-generated content? Does it prohibit the creator from using AI tools in any part of their process?

    Industry observers note that “We’ve had to specify that a few times just to make sure, because obviously you want the creator to be able to use AI tools in the background when they’re developing their concept or their script. Even utilizing AI to analyze their past performance of their content and advise them on their strategy moving forward. And I think brands should probably embrace that because it ultimately helps the creator deliver the best version of themselves and the best content possible,” said Stadelman.

    Here are a few highlights from the conversation, which have been edited for length and clarity.

    It’s way too risky to be only utilizing organic posting for creator campaigns and just hoping that the right people see it. We are seeing more and more brands utilize paid behind whether it’s white-listing or utilizing the creator content as an ad unit for themselves on their own channels. Along with that comes, obviously, you have to write the paid usage rights into the contract, and most brands are good about that.

    The wrong length for usage rights.

    Sources indicate that usage in perpetuity should never be agreed to. That’s a dangerous place to be for a creator and can negatively impact their future collaborations with other brands in the same category. Exclusivity, obviously, is quite difficult for a lot of creators if they agree to a longer exclusivity term than they should. That limits their options moving forward.

    The right length for usage rights.

    Sometimes you’ll see proposed terms that are just a little too lengthy with the usage rights. We push back on that sometimes. I don’t think there’s any reason to be agreeing upfront to any more than six months of paid usage. Even that’s a bit lengthy. Starting it at three months if they’re really wanting to utilize paid with the campaign, that makes sense. Even up to six months is fine in most cases. But once you get to that point six months from now, you can reassess and extend if you’d like. But I don’t think there’s any reason to go beyond that in the initial contract.

    It has been revealed that we always push for shorter payment terms. If somebody’s asking for net-90, we try to push for net-60 or, ideally, net-30. But I understand that some brands have their standard operating procedures there, which is fine. But we just ask that they honor those payment terms, which is a whole other issue that we’re seeing happen more and more, is that brands are just not honoring these payment terms that they’ve themselves written into the contract.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    Banking gets a helping hand in media modeling from SpendSight

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (790 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
    • It has been revealed that it’s easy to know what your bank balance is, in the age of apps and online banking.
    • Mediastruction, an independent media agency that two years ago introduced FutureSight, a SaaS platform dedicated to speeding up media mix modeling, is drilling into specific industries.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    It has been revealed that it’s easy to know what your bank balance is, in the age of apps and online banking. It’s not as easy for banks to know how effective their marketing efforts are.

    Mediastruction, an independent media agency that two years ago introduced FutureSight, a SaaS platform dedicated to speeding up media mix modeling, is drilling into specific industries.

    The brainchild of Marilois Snowman, who founded Mediastruction and FutureSight, SpendSight puts a specific lens onto the banking industry. It’s a free benchmarking tool that enables bank marketers to evaluate their media budgets to see if their spending aligns with their peers.

    It has been revealed that snowman mentioned conversations with clients and with other banks that aren’t yet clients told her there’s an information gap in the sector. “It’s a problem for mid market in general,” she explained in reference to other subscription media tools. “Sometimes mid-market brands don’t show up at all, or then they’re just wildly inaccurate.”.

    It has been revealed that for small banks, this information is pretty important, agreed Mark Gibson, marketing practice leader at Capital Performance Group. “It’s not uncommon in the banking industry to have one or two people in the marketing department, and maybe not even an ad or media agency,” he mentioned. “Media is like you know 1/20th of your job, so by definition, you’re not going to be very sophisticated about about what media is available and how you should allocate it. For that kind of advertiser, this kind of stuff can be really valuable.”.

    According to recent reports, snowman also noted that some media, from search to social and CTV, aren’t even properly tracked by other services. “Given the percentage of investment that is digital media these days — I mean, what isn’t digital media? — it just seems to be a major gap.”.

    Mediastruction built SpendSight from a proprietary 2026 survey of financial institution marketers, and Snowman said it’s the first of its kind to capture how banks and credit unions actually split paid media dollars across channels. To date, about 100 different banks and credit unions have participated in the survey, giving them access to the findings.

    In a recent development, any bank marketer enters their budget and channel mix, which lets SpendSight generate a side-by-side comparison against the peer average, flagging where they’re over- or under-invested. All inputs and responses to the survey remain anonymous and the underlying survey data is never exposed.

    “All of that kind of discussion is really helpful for marketing teams to bring to executive leadership, and then to be able to sell through shifts in media aims and modeling engagements,” mentioned Snowman.

    In a recent development, so what has SpendSight determined? Initial results show some patterns with how banks and financial services have been marketing, and which media channels they’re relying on. Although it comes as no surprise that digital performance channels make up about 51% of the average media mix, broadcast and traditional media (linear TV, radio, print, out-of-home) still account for roughly 38%. (Interestingly, the American Bankers Association’s Banking Journal cited more than 60% digital spend, which Snowman attributed to differing channel definitions.).

    Recent findings suggest that within digital, paid search and paid social represent more than one-fourth of average spend (13.7% and 13.0%, respectively). Paid search is the most widely used channel, with 96% of institutions investing in it. As for other media, direct mail makes up 7.4% of the average mix and is used by 82% of institutions, which is more than linear TV, display, and online video (as anyone knows who gets mail at home).

    Gibson at Capital Performance Group, which participates in multiple surveys for banking including SpendSight, noted the reason he thinks SpendSight goes one step farther. “While [other studies] provide some useful benchmarking in terms of how much banks spend overall, and what various media are used, they don’t quantify the spend by media mix or by media channel,” he said. “That’s the new innovation that this tool does.”.

    It also gives Mediastruction lead generation to build up its potential client base with financial firms, which Snowman acknowledged. “What we really want to sell through is FutureSight’s modeling. We can use this as a free tool to get to know us to offer something of benefit to potential clients, that’s what our goal is.”.

    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    In Graphic Detail: How shoppers are adopting AI for product research ahead of Black Friday

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (688 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
    • Marketers are shifting ad dollars toward performance channels as the notable Black Friday/Cyber Monday trading period approaches.
    • The places they find information about brands, the sources that information is based on, and what they do with that information are all changing.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Marketers are shifting ad dollars toward performance channels as the notable Black Friday/Cyber Monday trading period approaches. Yet the way consumers use search — a crucial channel within performance marketing — is evolving rapidly, as they adopt generative AI tools like Gemini and ChatGPT to aid their purchasing decisions.

    The places they find information about brands, the sources that information is based on, and what they do with that information are all changing. Meanwhile, audience adoption of AI research is far from uniform across generations and markets, further complicating the picture.

    “Black Friday used to be won in the final week with the deepest discount and the loudest media,” said Jonathan Verrall, vp of SEO at Jellyfish. “Now AI writes the shortlist weeks earlier from the sources shoppers trust. Advertisers who treat Black Friday as pure promo media are already late. The winners will proposal earned, owned and paid together from October and give AI data it can believe.”.

    What is certain is that the way brands seek to influence consumers during product discovery and research is shifting. With the year’s biggest sales event around the corner, read on for a data snapshot of the state of product discovery.

    According to a survey of 2,800 shoppers in the U.S. and U.K. conducted by Brainlabs in 2025 and 2026, the percentage of consumers using AI for product research rose on average from 6% last year to 13%. Clearly, more shoppers are using AI tools to compare and research the products they’re considering. While search engines themselves still led consumer practices, sources like Amazon and YouTube slipped.

    Industry observers note that A Jellyfish study of citation sources, using U.K. Black Friday-related prompts the week beginning Nov. 16, found third-party sources leading the pack. That means blogs, news articles and comparison sites counted for more than brands’ own websites or retail listings in influencing AI chatbot representations of a brand or a product.

    This is borne out by other studies. In an analysis run for an unnamed client, PMG found a brand’s website supplied just 24 out of 203 links cited in AI answers recommending the client’s products. Only 22 went directly to its homepage.

    Sources indicate that even if they only account for a minority of citations, brands’ own sites, platforms and retailer listings are areas that an advertiser can control. Zooming in, not all retail platforms are equal, either. Amazon, Costco and Etsy’s sites have lost share of citations in recent quarters, while Target and Walmart have gained in recent months, according to data from Tinuiti and Profound.

    Recent findings suggest that the hope that they might influence shoppers using AI tools for product discovery has been one of the motivations driving marketing dollars toward ChatGPT. Ad spend has risen month-on-month, according to estimates by AdClarity, which estimated total spend on the platform to have reached $116.6 million in October, with U.S. brands accounting for 64%. (The above chart is in millions of dollars.).

    Problems with measurability and evidence that ChatGPT ads lead to greater conversions, however, may hold brands back from accelerating that spend as much as OpenAI execs would like.

    Sources indicate that according to Bain, two-thirds of consumers use AI tools for general research, while 42% specifically use them to research products. But there are variations across generations.

    The McKinsey Agentic Commerce Consumer Survey, June 2026, surveyed 5,800 shoppers who’s used AI chatbots or search tools for a shopping task in the last three months. It found middle-aged and younger consumers are embracing the tech while older shoppers (who still hold plenty of disposable income) aren’t. It’s an notable distinction for brands targeting consumers in specific stages of their lives.

    As Black Friday Cyber Monday rapidly approaches, brands are most focused on acquiring upcoming customers this holiday season.

    Walmart is allowing access to Meta’s Muse through a gateway that lets it control how AI agents browse, shop and make purchases.

    Amazon is paying to reach ChatGPT shoppers while the chatbot is finding other ways to surface its products and deals.

    #124943. The clipping economy is changing as platforms crack down and creators seek control

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1303 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    The clipping economy is changing as platforms crack down and creators seek control

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1303 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
    • Depending on who you ask in the creator economy, they might say that clipping is dead.
    • Sources indicate that the practice of sharing short clips from long-form content to boost the original content’s audience or promote a brand, exploded in popularity over the last few years, with major creators like Jimmy “MrBeast” Donaldson, Cody “Clix” Conrod, and Eric “Airrack” Decker starting their own clipping companies.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Depending on who you ask in the creator economy, they might say that clipping is dead.

    Sources indicate that the practice of sharing short clips from long-form content to boost the original content’s audience or promote a brand, exploded in popularity over the last few years, with major creators like Jimmy “MrBeast” Donaldson, Cody “Clix” Conrod, and Eric “Airrack” Decker starting their own clipping companies. It catapulted certain creators into the spotlight and encouraged brands to hire clippers to give their branded partnerships extra airtime.

    In short, what began as fans sharing clips has grown into a billion-dollar distribution business.

    But some platforms are now tightening the rules around clipping. TikTok and YouTube have been cracking down on non-original and mass reposting content. Last week, Instagram added a content protection feature previously available only on Facebook, which lets eligible creators automatically identify videos matching their original content. They can now see how those videos perform and decide whether to hide them from people on the platform, add a credit link, or let the videos stay up. That gives creators more visibility and control over where their content appears, making clipping less of an open-ended reporting play and more subject to the original creator’s say.

    According to recent reports, “Creators deserve credit for the work they make,” a Meta spokesperson told Digiday. “[This] builds on our broader efforts to prioritize and reward original content and creativity over re-uploaded posts that don’t add a unique perspective or meaningful edits.”.

    And yet, platforms aren’t all moving in the same direction: Twitch is investing further into clipping to try and claw back the short-form real estate it’s ceded to other platforms. To understand what’s driving these diverging approaches, and what they mean in practice, Digiday spoke with seven experts across the clipping ecosystem.

    “Ask 10 people [what clipping is] and you’ll probably get eight different answers,” stated Darren Clover, CEO of creator-led holding firm Full Box Inc., which owns Reach Clipping. “We define clipping as skilled editors taking existing source material and transforming it into unique pieces of short-form content…Those videos are then distributed across individual social accounts. That’s very different from downloading someone else’s TikTok and reposting the exact same video across hundreds of accounts.”.

    Opinions also differ around whether clipping works as a performance marketing channel or if it’s just a good distribution method. A few days ago, Brian Blum, host of the Only Sweat Equity podcast, posted on X that clipping “has actually always been dead.” He told Digiday he meant that it has never worked as a performance marketing channel.

    Recent findings suggest that blum’s concern is that clipping can produce impressive view counts without reaching people likely to buy. He remarked campaigns can be vulnerable to fraud and attract audiences that may not be a fit for the product.

    “It doesn’t have necessary protections to prevent viewbotting or fraud…So you’re actually just lighting money on fire,” he said.

    Nikolai Amirzadeh, co-founded of clipping company Clip Tech, remarked clips can function as both marketing and distribution tools if the clipping company in question does the work to ensure views are valid.

    Sources indicate that “It is priced like performance, you pay per 1,000 verified views and nothing for clips that flop. It behaves like earned media, because it is native posts from real accounts, not ads. Brands typically pay $1 to $4 per thousand verified views, against $10 to $80 or more for traditional paid social,” Amirzadeh remarked. “Anything that looks off goes to the fraud team, and the clipper is not paid until it is cleared. A view is still a view by each platform’s own definition, which is a low bar. That is why the serious brands look at the top clips, watch time and what happens downstream, not just the view total.”.

    Then there’s the question of control: As clipping spreads and platforms tighten their rules, creators and their partners are increasingly concerned about how clips are edited and shared, and whether they could create brand-safety risks.

    “Clipping is kind of a double-edged sword. It can help creators gain visibility and show that people value their content, but it could also get them flagged as spam,” said Ashray Urs, head of Streamlabs.

    That lack of control gives creators and their managers pause, according to Reed Duchscher, CEO of Night Management. “It’s hard to control any of it,” he remarked. “Even when you put out a bounty for someone to clip something, you still have very limited control of what is posted, how it’s posted,” he added, pointing to the common practice of people clipping streamers out of context to farm outrage or drama.

    Instead, their clients, like mega creator Kai Cenat, have their own in-house clippers, which allows for more control and, crucially, legitimate measurement.

    Expect this to be an increasingly popular approach in the next year. “Sometimes with these clipping companies you can’t understand if the views are legitimate or not…you don’t know if they’re paid views or not paid views because you’re not controlling the TikTok accounts and not posting the videos. So we’re a little nervous about that,” Duchscher remarked.

    Recent findings suggest that with platforms cracking down on recycled content, the age of the clip farm may be over. But clipping itself isn’t.

    Sources indicate that mustafa Aijaz, vp of media company SoaR, thinks clipping is no longer a low-effort gold rush. “A quick cut and post won’t get you very far,” he stated. “You need a different caption, some commentary, or a breakdown — something that adds to the raw clip itself. If you’re different, the platform treats you differently. But if you look exactly like the other posts, you’ll likely be throttled.”.

    Recent findings suggest that and as the demand for clips has grown, some have leaned into the more negative aspects of clipping, like taking creators out of context or clipping moments that are less than flattering. This influx of negative framing or drama farming has shifted creators’ opinions on external clippers.

    Add that to the clipping companies’ increased selectiveness and rising rates, and something’s gotta give, according to Brandy Merriweather, founder and senior PR executive at BSTarPR.

    It has been revealed that “Many successful clipping pages have secured partnerships with gambling entities, music labels, creator management companies, creator collectives, and streaming platforms. Consequently, they are becoming more selective about which creators they post, their rates, and the frequency of posting for specific creators,” she mentioned.

    Merriweather told Digiday she’s seen creators have to pay extra money to clippers to switch priority streaming platforms.

    Sources indicate that “It’s a MAJOR business filled with egos, narrative control, fabricated numbers, unethical and sometimes purposely false content all going to the highest bidder,” she said. To avoid price gouging or unfair depictions, creators need to take clipping into their own hands. “What used to be a vehicle to gain visibility has now turned into an accountability stage that creators have no control over since many don’t own these pages. The creators, their families, and their teams are being used to create drama and fuel negativity which algorithms have prioritized because of the engagement….It’s a system many helped build that now controls them.”.

    Merriweather’s solution matches the other experts Digiday spoke with: creators have to create their own clipping networks to ensure they have control over their content and a proper understanding of how it’s performing.

    OpenAI revised its ChatGPT Business Hub terms following concerns that the original language could restrict businesses’ legal claims.

    Grand Theft Auto 6 has its own content creator cottage industry, with millions of views and a crowded, competitive marketplace.

    ChatGPT’s new AI visibility and click data can help inform publishers’ GEO strategies and complement third-party analytics.

    #124933. Digiday+ Research: A-Frame Brands, Ritual and other brands prioritize newly introduced customer acquisition this holiday season

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (560 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    Digiday+ Research: A-Frame Brands, Ritual and other brands prioritize newly introduced customer acquisition this holiday season

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (560 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
    • It has been revealed that this research is based on unique data collected from our proprietary audience of publisher, agency, brand and tech insiders.
    • As Black Friday and Cyber Monday rapidly approaches, brands are most focused on acquiring new customers this holiday season.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    It has been revealed that this research is based on unique data collected from our proprietary audience of publisher, agency, brand and tech insiders. It’s available to Digiday+ members. More from the series →.

    As Black Friday and Cyber Monday rapidly approaches, brands are most focused on acquiring new customers this holiday season. They’re also eager to turn those seasonal shoppers into repeat buyers.

    Fifty-nine percent of brand and retailer professionals said that new customers are the primary audience for their 2026 holiday advertising. That’s down just one percentage point from the 60% of marketers who said the same last year, indicating that customer targeting trends have not shifted significantly.

    Less than half of survey respondents (41%) mentioned that existing customers are the main audience for their holiday marketing, up one percentage point from 40% in 2025.

    The holiday season’s influx of shoppers gives brands an annual opportunity to attract new customers and to build lasting relationships beyond the initial purchase.

    Recent findings suggest that ari Bloom, founder and CEO of brand incubator A-Frame Brands, estimates that brands see a 20% to 30% increase in fresh customers as a percentage of total during the holiday season, as consumers look to discover products and brands. “It is a time period where you can acquire a lot of new customers… when we naturally see new customers come into the holiday funnel,” Bloom remarked.

    Recent findings suggest that he also expects AI to play a central role in 2026 holiday marketing, changing how consumers find and buy products. “AI is probably going to become one of the most crucial funnels for upcoming customers because, instead of using old habits to discover existing brands, there’s a whole other ‘person’ shopping for them,” Bloom said. “Just as we see people relying more on AI agents, you’re going to see more new brand exploration and customer acquisition from the brand side.”But acquiring new customers is only part of the equation. Brands also need to give existing customers a reason to return.

    Recent findings suggest that laura Brodie, chief growth officer at supplement company Ritual, said brands can encourage repeat purchases by offering exclusive perks, seasonal products and other incentives. “Being able to pull people back who have shopped before by creating a compelling gift with purchase, seasonal drop or something similar is one way,” Brodie said. “If you don’t have the budget to support units, having something that feels intentional for an existing customer base is another.”.

    Brands with similar consumer bases should also consider partnering on gift-with-purchase offers, according to Brodie. “The cost of acquisition is high during the holidays, so being able to tap an existing audience can be really cost-effective,” she remarked. “Similar-sized brands can create something that feels compelling [to consumers] and benefits both brands — potentially an offer swap. We’ve had success partnering with brands like Osea on a swap gift with purchases.”.

    Product discovery habits are changing, leaving marketers unsure how to pivot ahead of the biggest sales period of the year.

    Walmart is allowing access to Meta’s Muse through a gateway that lets it control how AI agents browse, shop and make purchases.
